T1: Individual users will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because they view it as a life-saving safety device for remote or emergency situations, and they are willing to pay a premium for reliability and compliance with NOAA/RTCM standards. Who benefits: Marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts, and individuals in remote areas who need reliable emergency communication.. Why behaviour changes: The Federal Register rule (2002) and NOAA guidelines make compliance mandatory, creating a regulatory barrier that only a certified device can clear, prompting consumers to choose a trusted brand over generic alternatives.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling a premium-priced, certified product through retail channels, leveraging its existing B2B reputation and the FCC waiver that allowed type certification for consumer use.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of the 406 MHz PLB capability and its regulatory requirements.; They trust ACR's brand and certification status.; The price premium is acceptable for safety-critical use cases.. Predictions: In a test offering a certified 406 MHz beacon at a price 20% above a generic alternative, purchase intent among marine recreational users will be at least 15% higher than for a non-certified generic beacon.; Surveyed buyers will cite 'NOAA certification' and 'satellite reliability' as primary purchase drivers..

T2: Individual users will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it offers convenience and real-time tracking, enabling them to stay connected with loved ones and receive rescue notifications, and they are willing to pay for the added safety and peace of mind. Who benefits: Travelers, outdoor workers, and families in remote areas who need continuous communication and rescue awareness.. Why behaviour changes: The rise of GPS and satellite communication makes real-time tracking desirable; consumers seek devices that provide continuous location updates and rescue notifications, creating a demand for a beacon that goes beyond a one-time emergency.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by positioning the beacon as a smart safety device with tracking and rescue capabilities, selling it through consumer electronics retailers and offering subscription services for real-time updates.. Assumptions: Consumers value continuous location tracking and rescue notifications over a single emergency signal.; The price premium for tracking features is acceptable for safety-conscious buyers.; ACR can integrate tracking software and data services into the product.. Predictions: In a test offering a tracked 406 MHz beacon at a price comparable to a standard PLB, purchase intent among outdoor workers will be at least 20% higher than for a non-tracked generic beacon.; Surveyed buyers will cite 'continuous tracking' and 'rescue notifications' as primary purchase drivers..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Emergency vs Tracking Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a product description emphasizing life-saving emergency capability (NOAA certification, RTCM compliance, suitable for remote or life-threatening situations). Group B sees the same description but emphasizes continuous tracking and real-time rescue notifications (GPS, location updates, rescue alerts). Both groups see a price point 20% above a generic PLB (e.g., €150). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and state the primary purchase driver.. Sample: 300 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced across gender and age to reflect marine recreational and outdoor user demographics. Recruitment targets individuals who have used a personal locator beacon or are interested in emergency safety gear.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary purchase driver (open-ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (price sensitivity).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Group B, and the majority of Group A buyers will cite 'NOAA certification' and 'satellite reliability' as primary drivers.; T2: Group B will show purchase intent at least 20% higher than Group A, and the majority of Group B buyers will cite 'continuous tracking' and 'rescue notifications' as primary drivers.. Decision rule: If Group A purchase intent ≥ 15% points higher than Group B, adopt T1‑driven consumer proposition (emergency capability). If Group B purchase intent ≥ 20% points higher than Group A, adopt T2‑driven consumer proposition (tracking/continuous). If the difference is ≤ 10% points, no expansion is recommended. If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a full consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows ACR already sells to individual buyers (e.g., marine recreational users) and has a B2B reputation, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand for tracking or willingness to pay a premium. Run the proposed test to measure purchase intent differences between emergency and tracking messaging. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer demand, purchase intent, or tracking capabilities for a 406 MHz satellite distress beacon. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a full consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows ACR already sells to individual buyers (e.g., marine recreational users) and has a B2B reputation, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand for tracking or willingness to pay a premium. Run the proposed test to measure purchase intent differences between emergency and tracking messaging. Target customer: Marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts, and individuals in remote areas who need reliable emergency communication.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon that meets NOAA/RTCM certification, offering life-saving emergency capability and compliance with regulatory requirements, sold through retail channels at a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Consumer Proposition Test (Emergency vs Tracking Messaging) within the 12‑week, €18,000 budget to measure purchase intent differences and determine whether to pursue a consumer proposition.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market, willingness to pay a premium for certification, and the competitive landscape for consumer PLBs are uncertain. The test will clarify these points.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the emergency messaging group at least 15% higher than for the tracking messaging group, we would adopt T1‑driven consumer proposition.; If the test shows purchase intent for the tracking messaging group at least 20% higher than for the emergency messaging group, we would adopt T2‑driven consumer proposition.; If neither condition is met and the difference is ≤ 10% points, we would recommend no expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

case.question: It is mid-1962. Should Deere & Company develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its tractor engineering? What evidence would justify that investment?

Homeownership of one-family detached homes rose significantly in the 1950s, modestly in the 1960s and 1970s, dropped slightly in the 1980s, and shows an extremely small increased in the 1990s, reaching 87 percent in 2000 (see graph).

An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
International Harvester introduced the Cub Cadet in 1961; Wheel Horse, Bolens, and Simplicity, to mention a few, were also dominate players before John Deere came onto the scene.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.
Lawn and garden equipment sales rise 76 percent.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.
Of the "10" series John Deere tractors introduced in 1960, the 4010 was by far the most popular, with more than 58,000 units sold from 1960 to 1963.
In 1869, Charles began to introduce marketing centers and independent retail dealers to advance the company's sales nationwide.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as market demand, technical feasibility, or competitive advantage.; Consider the existing B2B2C model of independent dealer distribution and the current reach to individual buyers.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming, or homeowner tasks) using tractor engineering.; 2) Expand the existing B2B2C model by deepening dealer relationships and offering additional service or parts to individual buyers without a new differentiated proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B2C model of farm and industrial equipment sold through independent dealers.; 4) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners, urban gardeners, or DIY enthusiasts) with a proposition tailored to their needs, using the same tractor platform..

T1: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated lawn tractor proposition because they view it as a convenient, single‑tool solution for small‑scale landscaping and gardening, and they trust the brand for durability and reliability. Who benefits: Individual homeowners with small gardens who need a single tool for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from multiple tools or manual labor to a single, easy‑to‑use machine that can handle multiple tasks, reducing time and effort.. How value is captured: Deere captures value by selling a differentiated model at a premium price through independent dealers, leveraging its tractor engineering to offer superior performance and durability.. Assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for a single, integrated tool.; Independent dealers can effectively promote and service the new proposition.; The market size for small‑scale landscaping is sufficient to justify production.. Predictions: A test offering a differentiated lawn tractor to homeowners will generate higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates compared to a generic garden tool.; Sales of the differentiated model will be concentrated among homeowners with small gardens, not large‑scale commercial users..

T2: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated lawn tractor proposition because they seek a single, integrated tool that reduces the number of tools they need to purchase and maintain, and they trust the brand for reliability. Who benefits: Individual homeowners who currently own multiple garden tools and are looking for a single, easy‑to‑use solution.. Why behaviour changes: They shift from owning multiple tools to a single machine that can handle multiple tasks, reducing purchase and maintenance costs.. How value is captured: Deere captures value by offering a differentiated model at a premium price through independent dealers, leveraging its tractor engineering to provide superior performance and durability.. Assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for a single, integrated tool.; Independent dealers can effectively promote and service the new proposition.; The market size for small‑scale landscaping is sufficient to justify production.. Predictions: A test offering a differentiated lawn tractor to homeowners will show higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates compared to a generic garden tool.; Sales of the differentiated model will be concentrated among homeowners who already own multiple garden tools, not those who need a single tool..

Test "Homeowner Preference Test: Single vs Multiple Tools" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a description of a differentiated lawn tractor positioned as a single, integrated tool for small-scale landscaping. Group B sees the same description but positioned as a tool that reduces the number of tools needed to purchase and maintain. Both groups view a generic garden tool. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and whether they would purchase the product.. Sample: 300 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness. Randomly assigned 150 to Group A and 150 to Group B.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and binary purchase decision (yes/no). Secondary measure: willingness to pay a premium over a generic tool.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates than Group B, because homeowners view the tractor as a convenient, single-tool solution.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates than Group A, because homeowners seek a single, integrated tool that reduces the number of tools they need to purchase and maintain.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 6.5 and Group B’s average ≤ 1.5), conclude T1 is supported. If Group B’s average is at least 5 points higher, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Therefore, the recommendation is to proceed with a test to measure homeowner preference before any Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

The evidence shows a growing lawn and garden equipment market and the success of the 4010 model, but it does not directly address whether homeowners view the tractor as a convenient, single-tool solution. Therefore, the recommendation is to proceed with a test to measure homeowner preference before any Target customer: Individual homeowners with small gardens who need a single tool for mowing, weeding, and light cleanup.. Value proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor positioned as a convenient, integrated solution for small-scale landscaping, offering superior performance and durability compared to generic garden tools.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Homeowner Preference Test (300 homeowners, 4 weeks, €2,000) to compare purchase intent and conversion rates for a differentiated lawn tractor versus a generic garden tool.. Uncertainty: The test will determine whether homeowners view the tractor as a convenient, single-tool solution (T1) or as a tool that reduces the number of tools they need to purchase and maintain (T2). The test is the primary source of evidence before. Would change if: If the test shows a difference of at least 5 points in favor of Group A (purchase intent for the differentiated model), the recommendation would shift to prioritize T1 and proceed with the differentiated proposition.; If the test shows a difference of at least 5 points in favor of Group B, the recommendation would shift to prioritize T2 and consider a proposition focused on reducing tool ownership.; If the test yields no significant difference or the difference is less than 1.5 points, the recommendation would remain to conduct further data collection or market research before committing to any expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Homeowner Preference Test: Single vs Multiple Tools" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a description of a differentiated lawn tractor positioned as a single, integrated tool for small-scale landscaping. Group B sees the same description but positioned as a tool that reduces the number of tools needed to purchase and maintain. Both groups view a generic garden tool. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and whether they would purchase the product.. Sample: 300 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representativeness. Randomly assigned 150 to Group A and 150 to Group B.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and binary purchase decision (yes/no). Secondary measure: willingness to pay a premium over a generic tool.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates than Group B, because homeowners view the tractor as a convenient, single-tool solution.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and higher conversion rates than Group A, because homeowners seek a single, integrated tool that reduces the number of tools they need to purchase and maintain.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 6.5 and Group B’s average ≤ 1.5), conclude T1 is supported. If Group B’s average is at least 5 points higher, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

T1: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it is marketed as a life-saving emergency device for remote environments, and they will purchase it if it is positioned as a premium safety tool for outdoor activities (e.g., hiking, camping, boating). Who benefits: Individual outdoor enthusiasts and recreational users who need reliable signaling in remote areas where traditional communication fails.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers will shift from generic emergency equipment to a dedicated beacon when they understand its unique capability to reach a distress call through satellite, offering peace of mind and higher perceived safety.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling premium-priced units directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or online channels, leveraging its existing brand credibility for marine and military safety.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of the existence and purpose of 406 MHz PLBs.; Outdoor activities in remote areas (e.g., Alaska, Australia) are common enough to create demand.; Willingness to pay a premium for a specialized device is higher than for generic ELTs.; ACR can reach individual buyers through existing channels or new partnerships.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer-focused marketing campaign to outdoor groups, purchase intent will exceed 10% among respondents who identify themselves as hikers, campers, or boating recreationists.; Surveyed consumers will cite 'safety in remote emergencies' as the top reason for purchasing the beacon, with willingness to pay at least $800..

T2: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade 406 MHz satellite distress beacon primarily because it is marketed as a cost-effective, no‑regulation alternative to expensive ELTs and RFFI, and they will purchase it when price is the primary barrier to entry. Who benefits: Budget‑conscious outdoor enthusiasts, boat owners, and emergency‑prepared individuals who need a reliable signaling device without the cost of professional certification.. Why behaviour changes: Buyers will switch from generic emergency equipment to a dedicated beacon when they perceive it as a cheaper, simpler solution that meets the same safety requirement without the regulatory and certification overhead.. How value is captured: ACR can capture value by selling lower‑priced units through mass‑market channels, leveraging its existing manufacturing capabilities to produce a consumer‑focused version of its existing product line.. Assumptions: Price is the primary barrier to adoption for emergency signaling devices.; Consumers are aware of the existence of 406 MHz PLBs but do not view them as a premium product.; ACR can produce a consumer‑grade version of its existing product at a lower cost than its current B2B offerings.. Predictions: In a test offering a low‑priced consumer version of the beacon, purchase intent will be higher among respondents who cite budget constraints as their primary reason for not buying a beacon.; Surveyed consumers will cite 'cost' as the top reason for not purchasing a beacon, with willingness to pay at least $500..

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Premium vs. Cost-Concern Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Recruit 400 respondents (200 self-identified outdoor enthusiasts/hikers, 200 budget-conscious consumers). Randomly assign participants to one of two message conditions: (A) premium positioning emphasizing life-saving capability and remote emergency use; (B) cost‑concern positioning emphasizing lower price and no certification requirement. Both conditions present a $800 price point for a consumer‑grade 406 MHz beacon. Measure purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and primary reason for not buying (open‑ended).. Sample: 400 respondents (200 outdoor enthusiasts, 200 budget‑conscious consumers) recruited via outdoor forums and general consumer panels.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and primary reason for not buying (open‑ended).. Predictions: T1: In the premium condition, purchase intent will be at least 10% among outdoor enthusiasts and at least 5% among budget‑conscious consumers; primary reason will be "safety in remote emergencies."; T2: In the cost‑concern condition, purchase intent will be at least 10% among budget‑conscious consumers and at least 5% among outdoor enthusiasts; primary reason will be "cost.". Decision rule: If purchase intent in the premium condition exceeds 10% among outdoor enthusiasts and 5% among budget‑conscious consumers, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If purchase intent in the cost‑concern condition exceeds 10% among budget‑conscious consumers and 5% among outdoor enthusiasts, consider a lower‑priced consumer version. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer sales.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Safety vs Protection Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of individual buyers interested in marine safety and outdoor equipment protection. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Safety-focused (emphasizing marine safety hazards and protective coatings as a medical necessity) or Protection-focused (emphasizing protection from marine elements and chemical damage). After viewing the message, participants are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: Proposed sample: 500 participants (250 per condition) from a panel of individual buyers interested in marine safety and outdoor equipment protection.. Measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each condition. Secondary measure: maximum price willingness to pay.. Predictions: T1: Safety-focused condition will yield higher average purchase intent and higher average maximum price than Protection-focused condition.; T2: Protection-focused condition will yield higher average purchase intent and higher average maximum price than Safety-focused condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the Safety-focused condition is at least 5 points higher than the Protection-focused condition (i.e., Safety ≥ Protection + 5), proceed with a safety‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 5 points, proceed with a protection‑focused proposition. If the difference is less than 2 points, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Differentiated vs. Compliant Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults aged 18-55, balanced across gender and geographic regions. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) style-focused, comfortable earplug marketed as a lifestyle accessory for concerts and outdoor activities; (2) compliant earplug marketed as a safety requirement for construction and hunting; (3) neutral control earplug with no messaging. All conditions present the same product description and price ($45). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 300 participants (100 per condition) to ensure statistical power and detect a 10% difference in purchase intent.. Measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each condition. Secondary measure: willingness to pay (EUR) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Style-focused condition will achieve the highest average purchase intent score (>=7.5) and willingness to pay compared to the neutral control.; T2: Compliant condition will achieve the highest average purchase intent score (>=7.5) and willingness to pay compared to the neutral control.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the style-focused condition is >=7.5 and significantly higher than the neutral control, conclude T1 is supported. If the average purchase intent score for the compliant condition is >=7.5 and significantly higher than the neutral control, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition meets the threshold, the evidence is insufficient to distinguish between the theories.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory, emphasizing comfort, style, and situational awareness. Begin with a limited pilot offering at concert doors and outdoor events to test purchase intent and willingness to pay. Use the results to decide whether to scale the differentiated offering or return to a standard product. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-A) concerns a wear test on appearance and does not address consumer willingness to pay, purchase intent, or regulatory requirements, which are central to T1. Therefore it does not affect the theory. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-A.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory, emphasizing comfort, style, and situational awareness. Begin with a limited pilot offering at concert doors and outdoor events to test purchase intent and willingness to pay. Use the results to decide whether to scale the differentiated offering or return to a standard product. Target customer: Consumers aged 18-55 who engage in concerts, outdoor recreation, and work in regulated environments, seeking comfortable, stylish protection.. Value proposition: A style-focused, comfortable earplug that combines hearing protection with a fashion-forward design, offering peace of mind and enhanced situational awareness for a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 6‑week, €18,000 online survey test with 300 participants, randomized to style‑focused, compliant, and neutral messaging conditions, to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources; no internal company data is available. The simulated result (SYN-A) concerns a wear test on appearance and does not address consumer willingness to pay, purchase intent, or regulatory drivers,. Would change if: If the test shows the compliant condition achieving >=7.5 purchase intent and willingness to pay, T2 would become more likely and the recommendation would shift toward a safety‑focused proposition.; If the test fails to meet the purchase intent threshold or shows no significant difference between conditions, the evidence would be insufficient to support either theory and the recommendation would remain unchanged.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection proposition if it is positioned as a lifestyle accessory that combines comfort, style, and safety, because they currently view hearing protection as a medical necessity and are willing to change behaviour when it is provided for free at entry points. Who benefits: Consumers seeking comfortable, stylish protection for activities like concerts, outdoor recreation, and leisure; Hellberg Safety gains premium pricing and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is presented as a fashion item and provided at no cost, consumers overcome the perceived discomfort and appearance concerns, leading to higher purchase intent and repeat use.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through premium pricing for stylish designs, direct-to-consumer sales, and repeat purchases of multiple pairs for different activities.. Assumptions: Consumers currently view hearing protection as a medical necessity rather than a lifestyle accessory.; Free provision at entry points (e.g., concert doors) increases willingness to try new products.; Hellberg can design and manufacture stylish, comfortable products that meet safety standards.. Predictions: In a test offering a stylish, comfortable hearing protection product at a concert door, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than a standard earplug.; Consumers will report higher satisfaction with the product compared to a standard earplug.; Repeat purchase rate for multiple pairs will be at least 15% within 12 weeks..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated hearing-protection proposition if it is marketed as a safety requirement for specific high-risk activities (e.g., construction, industrial, medical) because they already use hearing protection in these environments and trust the certification. Who benefits: Professional users and employers who need certified protection for work; Hellberg Safety gains credibility and can command premium prices for certified products.. Why behaviour changes: When hearing protection is framed as a mandatory safety requirement for a specific use case, professionals overcome the perceived discomfort and appearance concerns, leading to higher purchase intent and compliance.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value through premium pricing for certified products, B2B sales, and partnerships with safety regulators and employers.. Assumptions: Professional users already use hearing protection in their work environment.; Safety certification is a trusted signal for employers.; Hellberg can obtain and communicate relevant certifications effectively.. Predictions: In a test offering a certified hearing protection product for a specific high-risk activity, purchase intent will be at least 30% higher than a standard earplug.; Professional users will report higher compliance with safety regulations when using the certified product.; Repeat purchase rate for multiple pairs will be at least 20% within 12 weeks..

Test "Lifestyle vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults aged 18-45 who have purchased hearing protection in the past 12 months. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three conditions: Lifestyle Condition (stylish, comfortable design, free at concert entry), Safety Condition (safety certification for specific high-risk activity, mandatory requirement), and Control Condition (no messaging). In each condition, participants are shown a product description of a hearing protection item (Hellberg Junior) and asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10).. Sample: 300 participants (100 per condition), recruited from an online panel to ensure diversity in age, gender, and hearing protection purchase history.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for the Hellberg Junior product in each condition.. Predictions: T1: Lifestyle Condition will achieve a purchase intent score at least 20 points higher than Safety Condition.; T2: Safety Condition will achieve a purchase intent score at least 20 points higher than Lifestyle Condition.. Decision rule: If Lifestyle Condition’s purchase intent score is at least 20 points higher than Safety Condition’s, conclude T1 is more supported. If Safety Condition’s purchase intent score is at least 20 points higher than Lifestyle Condition’s, conclude T2 is more supported. If neither difference meets the 20‑point threshold, the evidence is insufficient to distinguish between the two theories and the recommendation will be to conduct further testing.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions Hellberg's hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory, emphasizing style, comfort, and safety. Begin with a limited pilot offering at concert entry points to test purchase intent and repeat purchase behavior. Use the proposed Lifestyle vs Safety Messaging Test to validate the hypothesis that lifestyle messaging drives higher purchase intent than safety-m Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions Hellberg's hearing protection as a lifestyle accessory, emphasizing style, comfort, and safety. Begin with a limited pilot offering at concert entry points to test purchase intent and repeat purchase behavior. Use the proposed Lifestyle vs Safety Messaging Test to validate the hypothesis that lifestyle messaging drives higher purchase intent than safety-m Target customer: Consumers aged 18-45 who purchase hearing protection for leisure activities such as concerts, outdoor recreation, and daily use.. Value proposition: A stylish, comfortable hearing protection product that combines safety certification with a lifestyle aesthetic, offering peace of mind and a fashion-forward option for everyday use.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Lifestyle vs Safety Messaging Test (300 participants, 3 conditions, 4 weeks) to measure purchase intent differences. If Lifestyle Condition's intent score is at least 20 points higher than Safety Condition's, proceed to develop a. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources; no source directly measures consumer willingness to pay for a lifestyle proposition. The test budget of €20,000 and 12-week timeline are assumptions for the proposed experiment.. Would change if: If the Lifestyle Condition's purchase intent score fails to meet the 20-point threshold relative to Safety Condition, the recommendation would shift to focus on safety messaging or no expansion.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for safety-certified products in specific high-risk activities, the recommendation would shift toward a safety-focused proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Homeowners will purchase a differentiated consumer lawn tractor because it becomes an affordable, convenient chore solution for small gardens and outdoor tasks, and Deere can capture value through premium pricing and brand differentiation. Who benefits: Individual homeowners with small gardens who previously lacked efficient outdoor equipment.. Why behaviour changes: Increased awareness of the convenience and practicality of garden tractors, combined with the desire for easier outdoor maintenance, makes ownership seem like a sensible purchase.. How value is captured: Deere can charge a premium price for a purpose-built consumer model, sell through independent dealers, and maintain brand prestige while capturing higher margins than standard farm equipment.. Assumptions: Homeowners perceive garden tractors as a legitimate chore tool rather than a farm necessity.; Independent dealers will stock and service the consumer model effectively.; Marketing can communicate the value proposition to potential buyers.. Predictions: A survey of homeowners will show a higher intent to purchase a consumer lawn tractor than a generic farm tractor.; Sales of the intended consumer model will exceed the sales of a comparable generic model in the same market.; Deere's consumer segment will generate higher profit margins than its farm segment..

T2: Small‑farm owners will adopt a differentiated consumer lawn tractor because it reduces labor costs and improves efficiency for light‑to‑moderate farming tasks, and Deere can capture value through volume sales and service contracts. Who benefits: Small‑farm owners with limited labor and budget who need efficient equipment for light‑to‑moderate tasks.. Why behaviour changes: Economic pressure to lower labor costs and the need for efficient equipment for light‑to‑moderate farming tasks makes a consumer‑grade lawn tractor seem like a cost‑effective investment.. How value is captured: Deere can sell through independent dealers, offer service and parts contracts, and capture volume sales while maintaining a premium price for a purpose‑built model.. Assumptions: Small‑farm owners are willing to invest in equipment that reduces labor costs.; Independent dealers can provide the necessary service and parts for a consumer model.; The market size for small‑farm owners is sufficient to justify production.. Predictions: A survey of small‑farm owners will show higher intent to purchase a consumer lawn tractor than a generic farm tractor.; Sales of the intended consumer model will exceed the sales of a comparable generic model among small‑farm owners.; Deere's consumer segment will generate higher revenue per unit than its farm segment..

Test "Consumer vs. Small-Farm Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Recruit 400 respondents: 200 homeowners with small gardens and 200 small-farm owners. Randomly assign participants to one of two message groups: Homeowner group receives a chore-focused proposition (e.g., 'Easily maintain your small garden with a Deere lawn tractor—save time and effort!'); Small-farm group receives a farming-focused proposition (e.g., 'Increase efficiency and reduce labor costs with a Deere small-farm lawn tractor'). Both groups view a product description of the same intended consumer model (e.g., a 1962-style Deere lawn tractor). Measure purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 1‑10 scale.. Sample: 400 respondents (200 homeowners, 200 small-farm owners) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 1‑10 scale.. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and WTP than small-farm owners, indicating demand for a chore-focused proposition.; T2: Small-farm owners will show higher purchase intent and WTP than homeowners, indicating demand for a farming-focused proposition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent of the Homeowner group is at least 10 points higher than that of the Small-farm group, conclude T1 is supported. If the average purchase intent of the Small-farm group is at least 10 points higher than that of the Homeowner group, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 points, both theories remain plausible and further testing is needed.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners with small gardens, leveraging the existing tractor engineering and independent dealer network. The evidence shows a 76% rise in lawn and garden equipment sales and the 4010's popularity, but it does not confirm homeowner demand for a chore-focused proposition. A targeted test is needed to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Neumann should create a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers beyond its existing professional studio range, or keep a single professional range for all customers, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.; Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage.; Alternatives must include no expansion, a differentiated home‑studio proposition, and a broader professional range.. T1: Home-studio creators and individual buyers purchase Neumann products primarily for professional quality and compatibility with existing studio gear, not for fashion or multiple-pair ownership. Who benefits: Neumann benefits by commanding premium prices and maintaining brand prestige among professionals.. Why behaviour changes: If creators perceive Neumann as the only compatible, high-quality option, they will choose it over cheaper alternatives, even if the price is higher.. How value is captured: Neumann captures value through premium pricing and brand loyalty, leveraging its professional reputation to justify higher costs.. Assumptions: Creators are price-sensitive and prioritize technical performance over aesthetics.; Compatibility with existing studio gear is a decisive purchase factor.; Professional reputation is a key differentiator in the home-studio market.. Predictions: In a survey, creators will rank compatibility and professional quality higher than price when choosing Neumann.; Willingness to pay for Neumann will be higher than for comparable non-Neumann products.; Purchase intent will be driven by the perception of Neumann as the only compatible, high-quality option..

T2: Home-studio creators and individual buyers purchase Neumann products because they seek a consistent, professional experience across devices and platforms, and are willing to pay for brand reliability and ecosystem integration. Who benefits: Neumann benefits by expanding its customer base and increasing average transaction value through cross-selling of related products.. Why behaviour changes: Creators prefer a single brand that works seamlessly with their existing gear and software, reducing the need to switch between products and simplifying workflow.. Test "Framing Test for Home Body-Fat Analyser" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of health-conscious adults (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Health Framing (device marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management) or Fitness Framing (device marketed as a fitness tracking device). Both conditions present the same product description and price (proposed €199). Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (1‑10 euros).. Sample: 300 health-conscious adults recruited online, balanced for age, gender, and BMI.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (continuous).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Health Framing condition compared to the Fitness Framing condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the Fitness Framing condition compared to the Health Framing condition.. T1: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat scale if it provides a clear, actionable health message and is marketed as a personal wellness tool, because health awareness in the 1990s makes them willing to invest in devices that measure body fat for weight management. Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking to manage weight and improve health.. Why behaviour changes: Increased media coverage of health risks (heart disease, diabetes) and the availability of portable devices make consumers view body fat as a measurable health metric, prompting purchase for personal use.. How value is captured: Tanita would capture value through premium pricing for a differentiated consumer product and potential recurring revenue from accessories or subscription services for health tracking.. Assumptions: Consumers in 1993 are motivated by health concerns and are willing to pay for devices that provide measurable outcomes.; Marketing can effectively communicate the health benefits of body fat measurement to home users.; The technology can be adapted to a consumer-friendly form factor without compromising accuracy.. Predictions: A survey of target consumers would show at least 30% indicating intent to purchase a home body-fat scale for weight management.; Sales of a consumer version would exceed 5,000 units within the first year in a key market (e.g., Japan or the US)..

T2: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat scale if it is marketed as a medical-grade tool for professional use, because clinics and health clubs already use Tanita equipment and trust the brand, creating a perceived credibility that transfers to home users. Who benefits: Professional healthcare providers and clinics that need accurate body-fat measurements for patient care.. Why behaviour changes: Clinics and health clubs already purchase and rely on Tanita scales for clinical accuracy, so a consumer version would be seen as a compatible, trusted extension of that equipment, reducing perceived risk and increasing willingness to adopt. How value is captured: Tanita would capture value through higher-margin sales to professional channels and potential licensing of the technology to medical device manufacturers, leveraging existing brand credibility.. Assumptions: Professional users are willing to recommend a consumer version to colleagues.; The consumer version can meet the same accuracy standards expected in clinical settings.; Marketing can position the product as a professional-grade tool for home use.. Predictions: Professional users would indicate intent to purchase a consumer version at a rate at least 20% higher than a generic home scale.; Sales of a consumer version would be concentrated in clinics and health clubs, with fewer than 10% of units sold to individual consumers..

Test "Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Recruit 500 participants (250 self-identified health-conscious adults and 250 professional users: clinics/health clubs). Randomly assign participants to one of two conditions: Condition A (health-focused) or Condition B (professional-focused). Both conditions present a home body-fat scale with identical features (foot-to-foot BIA, 1993 model). Condition A messaging emphasizes health benefits and personal wellness; Condition B messaging emphasizes clinical accuracy and professional compatibility. Measure purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (maximum price).. Sample: 500 participants (250 health-conscious adults and 250 professional users) recruited via online panels.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will achieve purchase intent ≥ 30% and higher willingness to pay than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will achieve purchase intent ≥ 30% and higher willingness to pay than Condition A.. Decision rule: If Condition A purchase intent ≥ 30% AND Condition A willingness to pay ≥ Condition B willingness to pay, conclude T1 is supported. If Condition B purchase intent ≥ 30% AND Condition B willingness to pay ≥ Condition A willingness to pay, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition meets its threshold, conclude neither theory is strongly supported.. Cost: 8000 euros, 4 weeks.

Test "Fashion vs. Free Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a fashion-focused description of Hellberg earplugs (style, comfort, aesthetics) or a free/discount offer for the same product. Participants are randomly assigned to one of the two conditions and then asked about purchase intent (1-7 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions (150 per condition).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the fashion condition compared to the free condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the free condition compared to the fashion condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent in the fashion condition exceeds the average purchase intent in the free condition by at least 1.5 points (e.g., fashion: 5.5 vs. free: 4.0), conclude T1 is supported. If the free condition exceeds the fashion condition by at least 1.5 points, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is within 1.5 points, the results are inconclusive and further testing is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Emergency vs Tracking Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a product description emphasizing life-saving emergency capability (NOAA certification, RTCM compliance, suitable for remote or life-threatening situations). Group B sees the same description but emphasizes continuous tracking and real-time rescue notifications (GPS, location updates, rescue alerts). Both groups see a price point 20% above a generic PLB (e.g., €150). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and state the primary purchase driver.. Sample: 300 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced across gender and age to reflect marine recreational and outdoor user demographics. Recruitment targets individuals who have used a personal locator beacon or are interested in emergency safety gear.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary purchase driver (open-ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (price sensitivity).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show purchase intent at least 15% higher than Group B, and the majority of Group A buyers will cite 'NOAA certification' and 'satellite reliability' as primary drivers.; T2: Group B will show purchase intent at least 20% higher than Group A, and the majority of Group B buyers will cite 'continuous tracking' and 'rescue notifications' as primary drivers.. Decision rule: If Group A purchase intent ≥ 15% points higher than Group B, adopt T1‑driven consumer proposition (emergency capability). If Group B purchase intent ≥ 20% points higher than Group A, adopt T2‑driven consumer proposition (tracking/continuous). If the difference is ≤ 10% points, no expansion is recommended. If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a consumer proposition yet. The evidence shows ACR's 406 MHz PLB is intended for emergency use and meets regulatory requirements, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand for tracking or willingness to pay a premium. Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test to measure purchase intent differences between emergency and tracking messaging before investing in a differentiated consumer line. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Creators' Willingness-to-Pay Survey" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home-studio creators and individual content creators. They view product mockups of Neumann studio microphones and audio interfaces, each with a different price point (e.g., €500, €1,000, €1,500). They are asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay and to rank the features they would prioritize (e.g., sound quality, ease of use, bundled accessories).. Sample: 300 participants (150 creators, 150 individual buyers) from home-studio communities and social media platforms.. Measure: 1) Average maximum price participants indicate they would pay for each product. 2) Share of participants who select 'sound quality' as the top priority. 3) Share of participants who select 'ease of use' as the top priority.. Predictions: T1: Creators will indicate higher maximum prices for Neumann products than for competitors, and 'sound quality' will be the top priority for a majority of participants.; T2: Creators will indicate higher maximum prices for Neumann products than for competitors, and 'ease of use' will be the top priority for a majority of participants.. Decision rule: If the average maximum price for Neumann products is at least €1,200 and 'sound quality' is the top priority for at least 60% of participants, proceed to develop a differentiated home-studio proposition. If the average maximum price is below €1,200 or 'ease of use' is the top priority for at least 60% of participants, keep the single professional range for all customers.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated home-studio proposition that emphasizes Neumann's professional-grade sound quality and reliability, positioning it as a premium tool for creators who value performance. Value proposition: A premium Neumann product line that delivers superior sound quality, reliability, and professional-grade features, justified by Neumann's reputation for pro audio excellence.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a safety necessity for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, medical). They will pay a premium for products that meet or exceed regulatory standards (EN 352) and offer comfort and situational awareness. Who benefits: Individual consumers who need reliable hearing protection for specific activities (hunters, shooters, children, workers).. Why behaviour changes: Regulatory requirements and the need for reliable protection create a demand for certified products; comfort and situational awareness reduce perceived discomfort, making the product desirable beyond basic compliance.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by pricing differentiated products at a premium, selling through specialized channels (outdoor retailers, online), and leveraging its brand reputation for safety and comfort.. Assumptions: Consumers are aware of and understand EN 352 standards.; Regulatory compliance is a key purchase driver for hearing protection.; Comfort and situational awareness are important attributes for extended wear.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated product for a specific use case, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard earplug.; Willingness to pay will be above the price of a standard earplug, indicating a premium..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a lifestyle or fashion accessory, especially for children and outdoor enthusiasts. They will choose products that are visible, shareable, and align with personal style, leading to multiple purchases. Who benefits: Individual consumers who value personal style and social sharing, particularly parents of children and outdoor enthusiasts.. Why behaviour changes: Social media and peer influence make visible, shareable products more attractive; children and outdoor users seek products that stand out and are easy to show off, increasing purchase frequency.. How value is captured: Hellberg can capture value by designing visually appealing, shareable products, selling through lifestyle retailers and online platforms, and leveraging social media marketing to build brand awareness.. Assumptions: Social media and peer influence significantly impact purchase decisions for hearing protection.; Parents and outdoor enthusiasts are willing to pay a premium for stylish, visible products.; Products can be marketed as fashion accessories rather than purely functional safety gear.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated product positioned as a fashion accessory, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard earplug.; Willingness to pay will be above the price of a standard earplug, indicating a premium for style..

Test "Differentiated Consumer Proposition Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized product exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 adults (18+), 250 parents of children under 12. Recruit via panel to match demographics.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: "Would you buy this product for a specific use case?" (binary: Yes/No). 2) WTP: "How much would you pay for this product?" (open-ended). 3) Messaging preference: "Which positioning resonates most?" (EN 352 safety vs. fashion accessory).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for a product positioned as EN 352-compliant hearing protection for outdoor recreation.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for a product positioned as a fashion accessory (e.g., colorful design, shareable) for children and outdoor enthusiasts.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for the EN 352 positioning is at least 15 percentage points higher than for the fashion accessory positioning, proceed with a differentiated safety-focused proposition. If the difference is <5 points, consider a differentiated proposition but validate further. If neither positioning achieves the 15-point threshold, do not invest.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes EN 352 compliance and comfort for specific use cases (e.g., outdoor recreation, medical). Begin with a small-scale online test to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-A) concerns wear frequency of a styled protector versus a plain one and does not address consumer demand for a differentiated proposition, willingness to pay, or positioning. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a safety necessity for a specific use case (e.g., outdoor recreation, medical). They will pay a premium for products that meet or exceed regulatory standards (EN 352) and offer comfort and situational awareness.. Evidence: SYN-A.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes EN 352 compliance and comfort for specific use cases (e.g., outdoor recreation, medical). Begin with a small-scale online test to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: Individual consumers who need reliable hearing protection for specific activities (hunters, shooters, children, workers) and are willing to pay a premium for certified safety products.. Value proposition: A differentiated product that meets EN 352 standards, offers superior comfort and situational awareness, and is positioned as a safety necessity for specific use cases, providing peace of mind and compliance.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 10-week online survey test (500 respondents, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for an EN 352 positioning versus a fashion accessory positioning.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for differentiated hearing protection and the exact willingness to pay for EN 352 compliance are unknown. The test will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the EN 352 positioning is at least 15 percentage points lower than for the fashion accessory positioning, we would reconsider the safety-focused proposition or explore alternative positioning.; If the test yields no significant difference between the two positioning, we would recommend further market research before committing to a differentiated proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available by late 2002 to justify ACR Electronics investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case built on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive landscape for a consumer product.; Must consider ACR’s existing B2B products (shipping, aircraft, military, marine) and its current reach to individual buyers.; Must assess regulatory and market feasibility of a consumer product using satellite distress beacons.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual users (e.g., marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts) with a dedicated product line and marketing.; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add a consumer‑focused version of the beacon for marine recreational users).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on current B2B customers and existing product portfolio.; 4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer products, capturing value through royalties rather than direct consumer sales..

T1: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade satellite distress beacon if they experience a direct life-saving incident or are aware of rescue success rates, because the perceived risk of drowning or being unreachable motivates them to purchase the technology. Who benefits: Surveyors and marine recreational users in high-risk areas who face life-threatening emergencies at sea.. Why behaviour changes: A personal emergency beacon directly reduces perceived risk and provides immediate rescue capability, creating a tangible safety benefit that drives purchase.. How value is captured: ACR can sell a differentiated consumer product at a premium price to individual buyers through retail channels, capturing value from the higher margin of direct consumer sales.. Assumptions: Life-saving success rates for PLBs in the United States are known and communicated to consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay a price premium for a personal emergency beacon.; ACR can reach individual buyers through retail or online channels.. Predictions: In a survey of marine recreational users, at least 30% will report having experienced a life-threatening emergency at sea, and 15% will indicate they would purchase a personal emergency beacon if priced at $300-$500.; Willingness to pay for a consumer-grade beacon will be positively correlated with stated risk perception (e.g., likelihood of drowning)..

T2: Individual buyers will adopt a consumer-grade satellite distress beacon if they perceive it as a status symbol or a status differentiator, because they seek to signal safety, preparedness, and ownership of a premium safety device. Who benefits: Affluent marine recreational users, outdoor enthusiasts, and early adopters who value brand prestige and social signaling.. Why behaviour changes: The purchase is driven by the desire to demonstrate safety, preparedness, and ownership of a high-end, premium safety device, rather than purely functional necessity.. How value is captured: ACR can sell a differentiated consumer product at a premium price through specialty retailers or online channels, capturing value from higher margin direct-to-consumer sales and brand positioning.. Assumptions: Status signaling and brand prestige are important purchase drivers for marine recreational users.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that signals safety and ownership.; ACR can reach affluent individual buyers through specialty channels.. Predictions: In a survey of marine recreational users, at least 20% will report that they would purchase a personal emergency beacon primarily for status reasons, and 15% will indicate they would pay a price premium of $500 or more.; Purchase intent for a consumer-grade beacon will be positively correlated with stated importance of status signaling and brand prestige..

Does not show: It does not show that individual marine recreational users would purchase a consumer-grade beacon, nor that they are motivated by personal emergency risk..

T1: Individual buyers will adopt Jotun's marine and protective coatings for residential marine safety and outdoor equipment protection if they perceive the technology as a medical necessity for safety, leading to higher willingness to pay and repeat purchases. Who benefits: Homeowners and outdoor enthusiasts who prioritize safety and durability for boats, yachts, and recreational vehicles.. Why behaviour changes: Growing awareness of marine hazards and the importance of protective coatings for safety creates a perceived need that motivates purchase beyond aesthetic or decorative purposes.. How value is captured: Jotun can capture value by positioning its marine technology as a safety solution, offering premium-priced products and direct-to-consumer sales through its brand, and potentially licensing the technology to consumer brands.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety-related marine coatings.; Jotun's marine technology can be effectively communicated as a safety product to individual buyers.; Direct-to-consumer sales channels can reach and convert individual buyers effectively.. Predictions: Individual buyers will show higher purchase intent and higher average order value when presented with safety-focused marketing.; Sales of safety-oriented marine coatings will increase in regions with higher awareness of marine safety risks.; Repeat purchase rates will be higher for safety-focused products compared to purely decorative products..

Why behaviour changes: Growing awareness of marine hazards and the importance of protective coatings for durability creates a perceived need that motivates purchase beyond aesthetic or decorative purposes.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for protective marine coatings.; Jotun's marine technology can be effectively communicated as a protective product to individual buyers.; Direct-to-consumer sales channels can reach and convert individual buyers effectively.. Predictions: Individual buyers will show higher purchase intent and higher average order value when presented with protective-focused marketing.; Sales of protective-oriented marine coatings will increase in regions with higher awareness of marine environmental risks.; Repeat purchase rates will be higher for protective-focused products compared to safety-focused products..

Test "Safety vs Protection Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of individual buyers interested in marine safety and outdoor equipment protection. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: Safety-focused (emphasizing marine safety hazards and protective coatings as a medical necessity) or Protection-focused (emphasizing protection from marine elements and chemical damage). After viewing the message, participants are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: Proposed sample: 500 participants (250 per condition) from a panel of individual buyers interested in marine safety and outdoor equipment protection.. Measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each condition. Secondary measure: maximum price willingness to pay.. Predictions: T1: Safety-focused condition will yield higher average purchase intent and higher average maximum price than Protection-focused condition.; T2: Protection-focused condition will yield higher average purchase intent and higher average maximum price than Safety-focused condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the Safety-focused condition is at least 5 points higher than the Protection-focused condition (i.e., Safety ≥ Protection + 5), proceed with a safety‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 5 points, proceed with a protection‑focused proposition. If the difference is less than 2 points, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions Jotun's marine and protective coatings as a safety solution for residential marine safety and outdoor equipment protection. Use direct-to-consumer sales through the Jotun brand and leverage existing Multicolor centers to reach individual buyers. Conduct a small-scale test to validate purchase intent and price sensitivity before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions Jotun's marine and protective coatings as a safety solution for residential marine safety and outdoor equipment protection. Use direct-to-consumer sales through the Jotun brand and leverage existing Multicolor centers to reach individual buyers. Conduct a small-scale test to validate purchase intent and price sensitivity before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners and outdoor enthusiasts who prioritize safety and durability for boats, yachts, and recreational vehicles.. Value proposition: Jotun's marine technology is positioned as a safety solution, offering premium-priced products that protect against marine hazards, and enabling direct-to-consumer sales to capture higher margins and build brand trust.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Safety vs Protection Messaging Test (500 participants, 12 weeks, €20,000) to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity. Use the decision rule: if Safety purchase intent is at least 5 points higher than Protection, move. Uncertainty: The actual demand for safety-oriented marine coatings among individual buyers is unknown. The test will provide data on purchase intent and price sensitivity, but it does not confirm market size or willingness to pay.. Would change if: If the test shows the Protection-focused condition achieving a higher purchase intent score than the Safety-focused condition by at least 5 points, the recommendation would shift to a protection-focused proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference in purchase intent between the two conditions, further market research would be needed to understand consumer motivations.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Assumptions: Individual boat owners are willing to pay a premium for proven marine performance.; Jotun’s reputation in professional marine markets transfers to consumer perception.; The market size for individual boat owners is sufficient to justify investment.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated marine‑focused product at a premium price, at least 30% of surveyed individual boat owners will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales conversion rate will be higher than for a generic marine product of similar price point..

T2: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts will adopt Jotun’s decorative coatings if they perceive them as stylish, easy to apply, and affordable compared to competitors, because they seek aesthetic improvement for their homes. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently choose decorative paints based on price and availability; a differentiated proposition that highlights design options, ease of use, and competitive pricing will shift their preference from generic to brand‑specific. How value is captured: Jotun can expand its consumer presence through direct‑to‑consumer sales, retail partnerships, and potentially licensing its decorative brand to other retailers.. Assumptions: Residential buyers are willing to pay a premium for aesthetic appeal and ease of application.; Jotun’s decorative capabilities can be effectively marketed to DIY consumers.; The residential market size is large enough to justify investment.. Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Marine vs Decorative" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a marine‑focused product description or a decorative‑focused product description, followed by a purchase intent question.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 self‑identified individual boat owners and 250 self‑identified homeowners, recruited via panel to match age, gender, and geographic distribution.. Measure: Purchase intent: binary “Would you buy this product?” and willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale.. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of marine‑exposed respondents will indicate purchase intent and WTP above the decorative‑exposed baseline (25% intent, €150 WTP).; T2: At least 25% of decorative‑exposed respondents will indicate purchase intent and WTP above the marine‑exposed baseline (25% intent, €150 WTP).. Decision rule: If the marine‑exposed group’s purchase intent rate exceeds the decorative‑exposed group’s rate by at least 5 percentage points and its WTP is at least €50 higher, proceed with a marine‑focused consumer proposition. If the opposite holds, proceed with a decorative‑focused proposition. If both groups’ intent rates are equal and neither meets the 5‑point difference, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated marine‑focused consumer proposition for individual boat owners, leveraging Jotun’s marine‑grade reputation and professional endorsement. Use the proposed Consumer Proposition Test to validate demand before scaling. If the test shows a meaningful purchase intent advantage for marine‑exposed respondents, proceed with a marine‑focused launch; otherwise, reconsider the consumer expansion route. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer demand, purchase behaviour, or price sensitivity for marine coatings. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Use the proposed Consumer Proposition Test to validate demand before scaling. Target customer: Individual boat owners and marine enthusiasts who purchase marine‑grade coatings for their vessels.. Value proposition: A branded marine‑focused product that emphasizes proven durability, professional endorsement, and premium quality, enabling Jotun to capture higher margins through direct‑to‑consumer sales.. Uncertainty: The strength of consumer demand for marine coatings and the willingness to pay a premium for marine‑grade products is uncertain. The test will resolve this, but it is based on limited public evidence and simulated results.. Would change if: If the test shows the decorative‑focused group’s purchase intent rate exceeds the marine‑focused group’s rate by at least 5 percentage points and its WTP is at least €50 higher, we would reconsider the marine‑focused proposition and explore; If the test shows neither group meets the 5‑point difference and neither meets the €50 WTP threshold, we would conduct further market research before committing to any consumer expansion.. sources.excerpt: Based on medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes and certain cancers, Tanita introduced the world’s first integrated body composition analyzer/scale to the professional markets in 1992.
Tanita is a world leader in precision electronic scales. With almost 50% of its domestic market share, the name Tanita is a household name in Japan.
In Japan, every household has a bathroom scale (health meter), and most nowadays keep track of your body composition.

A body fat measuring apparatus for measuring body fat in a patient's body comprises apparatus for simultaneously measuring an impedance between the patient's feet, and for measuring the patient's height and the patient's weight

the impedance value of a body to be measured vary according to the date, time and differences of body condition before measurement. These various are too large to use the above-described inference formula accurately and amount of body fat calculated by the formula is likely to be inaccurate.
In 104 men and 101 women (16-78 years and BMI 16-41 kg/m2) the mean bias in body-fat mass measured using the Tanita body-fat analyser was 0.8 (2SD 7.9) kg relative to a four-compartment model.

This method is safe, noninvasive, provides rapid measurements, requires little operator skill and subject cooperation, and is portable. Further validation of this method is recommended in subjects with abnormal body composition.
The Tanita TBF-310 foot-to-foot BIA body composition analyser with the manufacturer's prediction equations is not recommended for application to individual children who are overweight and obese

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in 1993 to justify Tanita investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, building on its stand‑on bioelectrical impedance body‑fat analyser, by evaluating demand, market fit, competitive landscape, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before 1993; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning; no financial data available.; Any recommendation must be based on observable market behavior, not speculation about future outcomes.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home users for a specific use case (e.g., weight management, fitness tracking).; 2) Expand the existing B2B offering by adding new features or marketing channels to clinics and health clubs without a consumer focus.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market (clinics and health clubs).; 4) License the technology to third‑party manufacturers to create consumer devices, capturing value through royalties rather than direct sales..

T1: Consumers will adopt a home body-fat analyser if it is marketed as a health monitoring tool for weight management, because they already use bathroom scales and seek measurable health data. Who benefits: Home users who want to track weight and body composition for health improvement.. Why behaviour changes: If the device provides a clear, measurable health metric (body fat percentage), consumers will be motivated to purchase it as a tool to monitor progress and make informed health decisions..
